preamble: In French, the Old French diphthong ie came from Bartsch's law (Latin stressed a after a palatal: mercātum > marchié) and from diphthongization of ĕ, and was later pronounced [je]. The glide was then lost in most words. It was absorbed by a preceding palatal consonant or removed by analogy in -er verbs, and survived only where nasalization followed (chien [ʃjɛ̃]). The result merged with the e from the general fronting of a. In open final syllables the outcome is close [e], as in the infinitive ending -er and in nouns such as marché and congé. In closed syllables it later opened to [ɛ] (cher [ʃɛʁ], chef [ʃɛf]), which is a separate step.

examples.note: [ie] > [je] > [e] in the infinitive ending -ier after a palatal.
The glide was absorbed by the preceding palatal; -ier > -er spread analogically to other first-conjugation verbs.
Bartsch's-law ie after the palatal ch reduced to final [e].
